tagline: Birthplace of wine beneath the Caucasus
overview:
Georgia is a country on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, tucked beneath the towering Caucasus Mountains where Europe and Asia meet. It borders Russia, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Türkiye and is about 69,700 km², roughly the size of Ireland, with about 3.7 million people. It is not related to the US state of the same name; Georgians call their country Sakartvelo.

The capital, Tbilisi, was founded on hot sulfur springs about 1,500 years ago, and its name comes from the Georgian word for "warm." Old wooden balconies, a medieval fortress and modern glass buildings line the Kura River. Georgians speak a language unrelated to any other major language family, written in a curly alphabet of their own.

Georgia is a republic with an elected parliament. Two regions, Abkhazia and South Ossetia, broke away in the 1990s and are backed by Russia; Georgia and most of the world still consider them Georgian territory. The country is famous for feasting, wine, singing and mountain villages topped with stone towers.
landAndNature:
The Greater Caucasus forms Georgia's northern wall, with peaks such as Shkhara, about 5,190 meters, permanently capped in snow. In the high region of Svaneti, villages like Ushguli, one of the highest year-round settlements in Europe, are guarded by medieval stone towers. The Lesser Caucasus rises in the south, and between the two ranges lie fertile valleys of vineyards and orchards.

Along the Black Sea coast, the climate is humid and subtropical, with tea plantations and citrus groves around Batumi, while the east is drier. Georgia's limestone holds some of the deepest caves ever explored. Brown bears, wolves, lynx, chamois and the East Caucasian tur, a wild goat with sweeping horns, live in the mountains, and bearded vultures soar above the gorges.
peopleAndCulture:
Georgians are famous for the supra, a feast where a toastmaster called the tamada leads round after round of toasts to friendship, family and homeland. The table overflows with khachapuri, boat-shaped bread filled with molten cheese and egg; khinkali, twisted dumplings eaten by hand; and walnut sauces, herbs and pickles. Wine has been made here for about 8,000 years, fermented in huge clay jars called qvevri buried underground.

Most Georgians belong to the Georgian Orthodox Church, and ancient churches crown many hilltops. Polyphonic singing, in which several voices weave together without instruments, is so distinctive that UNESCO lists it as a cultural treasure. Wrestling, rugby and chess are popular, and the national ballet dancers leap and spin on the tips of their toes in soft boots.
history:
In Greek myth, Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis, in western Georgia, to steal the Golden Fleece, and real kingdoms of Colchis and Iberia thrived there in ancient times. Georgia adopted Christianity in the early 300s, one of the first countries to do so. Its Golden Age came in the 1100s and 1200s under King David the Builder and Queen Tamar, when Georgian culture and power reached their peak.

Mongol, Persian and Ottoman invasions followed, and in 1801 the Russian Empire began absorbing the Georgian kingdoms. A brief independence from 1918 to 1921 ended when the Soviet Red Army took control; the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin was born in the Georgian town of Gori. Georgia declared independence in 1991. Wars in Abkhazia and South Ossetia, the peaceful Rose Revolution of 2003 and a short war with Russia in 2008 have shaped its recent history.
funFacts: Fossils of early humans found at Dmanisi are about 1.8 million years old, the oldest ever discovered outside Africa.
Georgian is written in one of only about 14 alphabets in use in the world today, and it has no capital letters.
Archaeologists have found traces of wine in Georgian pottery from around 6000 BC, the oldest evidence of winemaking anywhere.
The world's deepest known caves, more than 2,200 meters deep, lie in the Arabika Massif of Abkhazia.
Tbilisi's name comes from "tbili," meaning warm, after the natural hot springs where the city was founded.
A traditional Georgian supra can include dozens of toasts, and the tamada must think of a new one every time.
